To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
water supply affects the yield response of wheat and its response to fertilizer, and that this is so for both freshly- and previously applied fertilizer.
the response of wheat to P fertilizer is affected by the water supply during the growing season, and that this response can be predicted by the P concentration in the dried tops of plants.

water stress reduces the effectiveness of rock phosphate and other P fertilizers, and that the effectiveness of P fertilizers is reduced when fertilizer is applied in the subsoils rather than in the surface soil.

developing a fertilizer recommendation system for the application of freshly- and previously- applied rock phosphate and super-phosphate.
the effect of water supply, as well as the placement of P fertilizers on the yield response of wheat and the residues of rock phosphate and/or superphosphate applied to the field.
the effects of water supply on crop response to rock phosphate and super phosphate, and on the residual effectiveness of these fertilizers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of water stress depends on the P fertilizer, its source, and its application history.
water supply affects the effectiveness of rock phosphate and the effectiveness of superphosphate.
the response of wheat to P fertilizers depends on the interaction between soil P, P fertilizer applied, and water supply.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
water supply affects the response of wheat to P fertilizers.
, for wheat and triticcale, the yield responses to rock phosphate and super phosphate are affected by water supply.
, in general, water stress reduces the effectiveness of P fertilizers by reducing the maximum yield potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fertilizer effectiveness, critical P, and soil test P calibration vary with water supply, which varies within and between seasons.
